description: Solo builder from India taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. I'm building HorizonLine: a web tool that lets anyone compare Moon south-pole landing sites by sunlight and Earth visibility in seconds, using NASA LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons data. My focus: UI design, data visualization and storytelling. Goal: make lunar mission planning simple and visual.
summary:
HorizonLine is a free web tool that helps compare potential lunar south-pole landing sites and landing dates based on two critical factors: sunlight for power and a clear line of sight to Earth for communication.

Landing near the Moon's south pole isn't simple. The Sun stays close to the horizon, meaning even a small crater rim or nearby hill can determine whether a lander gets weeks of sunlight or spends days in darkness.

HorizonLine uses NASA's LOLA terrain data to map the actual horizon around each landing site and JPL Horizons to simulate the movement of the Sun and Earth hour by hour from 2027 to 2029.

It includes NASA's Artemis III candidate regions, the IM-2 landing target, Chandrayaan-3, and any custom location selected directly on the map.

Whether you're a mission planner, student, or simply curious about lunar exploration, HorizonLine makes it easy to understand which location offers the longest periods of sunlight, when Earth disappears behind the lunar terrain, and how long a lander might remain in darkness.
details:
HorizonLine

What it does

HorizonLine helps compare potential lunar south-pole landing sites and landing dates based on two things a lander depends on most: sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication.

Here's what you can do with it:

  • Compare up to 3 landing sites side by side, looking at:
    • Average share of the Sun's disk visible above the horizon
    • Maximum Sun elevation
    • Percentage of time Earth remains visible
    • Longest period without sunlight
    • Longest communication blackout
  • Explore a 360° view of the lunar horizon. Watch the Sun and Earth move across the actual skyline throughout your selected stay. A live readout also tells you when the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset or Earthrise will happen.
  • Find the best landing window. A daily sunlight calendar covering 2027–2029 makes it possible to compare dates, not just locations.
  • Explore your own locations. Click anywhere on the south-pole map or enter coordinates, and HorizonLine will calculate the surrounding horizon directly in your browser.
  • Explore 11 existing locations: NASA's 8 Artemis III candidate regions, the IM-2 (CLPS) target, the Chandrayaan-3 landing site and Apollo 11 as a historical comparison.

How it works

I wanted HorizonLine to show what a lander would actually experience at the surface, rather than relying on general sunlight estimates.

1. Mapping the lunar horizon

For each location, I traced 720 directions, spaced 0.5° apart, through NASA's 80 m LOLA south-pole terrain model. The calculations account for the Moon's curvature and represent the skyline as seen from a lander's 2 m mast.

2. Tracking the Sun and Earth

I used JPL Horizons to obtain hourly positions and distances for the Sun and Earth. These are converted into Moon-fixed Sun directions and Earth positions.

The browser then calculates where both bodies appear in the sky from each landing site, including Earth's parallax.

3. Calculating the scores

For every hour, HorizonLine checks how much of the Sun's disk is visible above the local terrain and whether Earth has a direct line of sight.

It then combines these measurements across the selected stay to calculate sunlight availability, communication coverage and the longest periods of darkness and communication loss.

How I validated it

I didn't want to build something that simply looked convincing. I also wanted to check whether the calculations were producing reliable results.

Here are some of the checks I ran:

  • Sky calculations: Compared HorizonLine's results against Horizons' own per-site output, with differences below 0.0002° across all 8 Artemis III sites.
  • Earth direction: Verified the calculated direction against the geometric direction to the sub-Earth point, with differences below 0.1°.
  • Sun elevation: Checked the maximum Sun elevation against the theoretical value of 90° − latitude + 1.54°.
  • Sunlight availability: All 8 Artemis regions show 17–28 days of continuous sunlight, consistent with NASA's selection criterion of at least 6.5 days.

A couple of examples make the results easier to understand:

  • A location on the Shackleton rim receives 14 consecutive days of full sunlight.
  • At Apollo 11, the Sun reaches approximately 69° above the horizon. Near the lunar south pole, it never rises much above 5°.

An important limitation

One thing I discovered while testing HorizonLine is just how much terrain resolution matters.

When I compared different terrain resolutions against the 80 m model, coarser terrain made locations appear significantly sunnier:

  • At 240 m resolution, the score could increase by up to 11 percentage points.
  • At 960 m resolution, it could increase by up to 22 percentage points.

That's a substantial difference when planning a mission around solar power.

For this reason, I use the full 80 m terrain data for the curated locations. Custom locations are marked as approximate because their terrain calculations may be less reliable.

HorizonLine is also not a landing-safety assessment. It does not evaluate slopes, boulders or other surface hazards.

What makes it creative

Most landing-site visualizations give you a map and label locations as good or bad.

I wanted to approach the problem differently.

With HorizonLine, you can essentially stand at a potential landing site and watch the Sun and Earth move across its actual lunar skyline. You can see the exact moment the Sun disappears behind a crater rim or Earth drops below the horizon.

Instead of asking users to trust a score, HorizonLine lets them see why that score exists.

Factors I considered

The project focuses on five practical questions:

  • How much sunlight can a lander actually receive?
  • How reliably can it communicate directly with Earth?
  • What's the longest period it must survive without sunlight?
  • When is the best time to land, not just the best place?
  • How much does terrain resolution affect the final result?

Benefits and intended impact

HorizonLine is a free, open first-look tool that runs directly in a web browser, with no installation or login required.

Students, researchers, mission planners and anyone interested in lunar exploration can use it to understand the trade-offs between sunlight, communication and landing dates within seconds.

It isn't intended to replace detailed engineering analysis. Instead, it provides an accessible starting point before committing time and resources to more computationally intensive studies.

I also wanted it to make one thing easier for the general public to understand: landing near the lunar south pole isn't just about finding a flat place to land. It's about finding a place where a spacecraft can survive, generate power and stay connected to Earth.

What’s next

  • Extend HorizonLine to the lunar north pole and to any landing site NASA’s Artemis and CLPS missions announce next.
  • Plan rover routes that stay in sunlight and in contact with Earth, not just single landing points.
  • Add surface temperature and slope, so power, communication, heat and safety can be compared in one place.
  • A classroom mode, so students anywhere, including here in India where Chandrayaan-3 inspired millions, can explore real NASA and ISRO landing sites in their browser.

Tools and technologies

  • Scientific computing: Python, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, PyProj and Pillow
  • Frontend: JavaScript, D3.js, HTML and CSS
  • Astronomical data: JPL Horizons API
  • Terrain data: NASA LOLA
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages

AI assistance
I used Claude (Anthropic) for brainstorming, research, coding, data checks and drafting text. I made the final decisions, ran the NASA data downloads and Horizons queries, and reviewed every result.
Demo video voice-over generated with ElevenLabs (AI voice); the video was filmed and edited with AI assistance and carries a visible AI watermark.
